      <title>Arsenal 2-1 Leeds: Premier League – live</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/football/live/2026/oct/10/arsenal-v-leeds-premier-league-live</link>
      <description><p>⚽ Updates from the Emirates: kick-off 12.30pm BST<br>⚽ <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/oct/09/premier-league-10-things-to-look-out-for-this-weekend">Ten things to look out for</a> | <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/live">Live scores</a> | <a href="mailto:barry.glendenning@theguardian.com">Mail Barry</a></p><p><strong>An email:</strong> “Happy Saturday, Barry,” writes Mark Kerry. “Is it just me or are there other baffled Arsenal fans out there regarding Arteta’s obsession with starting Havertz as a centre forward? I just can’t see the rationale for it at this point, given that Havertz has proven over the last few seasons that he’s not at all prolific, whereas Gyokeres is clearly a capable finisher - as exemplified both by last season in the Premier League but also during recent internationals. Would Arsenal not be better to persist with, or even adapt to,a more natural goal scorer?”</p><p>I’m not an Arsenal fan, baffled or otherwise, but I don’t think Gyokeres is a good enough centre-forward to play for them and I’m not sure he’s done anywhere near enough to convince Mikel Arteta otherwise. His forte is running behind into the kind of space Arsenal just aren’t afforded by most teams they play against and for such a big unit, his hold-up play is dismal. It doesn’t surprise me that Kai Havertz is picked ahead of him.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/live/2026/oct/10/arsenal-v-leeds-premier-league-live">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>Goal averages are crumbling as players take fewer touches in the box and forwards underperform against xG</p><p>Goals are on the up in the Premier League. Matches have averaged 2.88 non-penalty expected goals, the second most in the past six seasons. Chances have been going to waste.</p><p>If the 20 teams converted at the par rate, there would have been almost two extra goals per week.       <title>‘Is the greatness of the Premier League a myth?’: Ed Aarons answered your football questions</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/sport/live/2026/oct/08/football-qa-ask-ed-aarons-your-questions-as-the-premier-league-returns</link>
      <description><p>With the Premier League back on Saturday, football writer Ed Aarons answered your questions on what the Man City verdict means, whether referees will be stricter, and whether Don’t Look Back In Anger was prophetic</p><p><strong><a href="https://discussion.theguardian.com/comment-permalink/175766661">Fearandloathingpart2</a> asks</strong>: Given the political pressure that is inevitably going to be placed on Man City, do you think the independent regulator will take action? If they don’t, they lose any credibility but it just seems unlikely to me they’ll take serious action against the ownership. Am I being too cynical? Any thoughts?</p><p><strong><a href="https://modtools.discussion.gutools.co.uk/discussions/p/x66cc3?page=2#comment-175768036">MademoiselleK</a> asks:</strong> Surely given the guilty verdict on City they should be suspended for the rest of the PL season pending the outcome of their appeal. Only five games in the PL could simply annul the results so far and drop to a 37 club competition. If they are allowed to play on then what happens when their appeal fails - presumably months down the line. Docking them points at that stage makes the league a joke as you will have a club whose serial cheating has already ruined the credibility of English football’s showcase competition which is watched by billions worldwide.</p><p><em><strong>Ed says:</strong> I don’t think you’re being too cynical, although it must be said this is probably the biggest challenge the new Independent Football Regulator (IFR) chair David Kogan could possibly ever have faced and it has come less than a year after he was appointed to the new role… The IFR is able to re-assess the suitability of owners, directors and executives and Kogan said in a statement that “we will use these powers where appropriate, in the interests of protecting the sustainability, honesty and integrity of English football where there is clear evidence of wrongdoing by individuals.”</em></p><p><em>However, the political ramifications that were highlighted by the reaction to Andy Burnham’s comments last week that he would be “really concerned” to lose the City’s owners from Abu Dhabi were an indication that this all goes well beyond football. It puts the IFR in a tricky situation, although it is meant to be independent and Kogan will be keen to show that.</em></p><p><em><strong>Ed says:</strong> There has already been an interesting case involving the team that you may be referring to in your question if my instinct serves me right?! The decision to award Sunderland a penalty against Arsenal last month enraged Mikel Arteta and his reaction was probably an attempt to try and put doubts in the officials’ minds the next time they are confronted with a similar situation. Quite clever really given how many goals Arsenal scored from corners last year… Referees are definitely on the lookout for miscreants at set pieces but actually cracking down on such chaos is not going to be easy without help from the VAR. Time will tell.</em></p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/sport/live/2026/oct/08/football-qa-ask-ed-aarons-your-questions-as-the-premier-league-returns">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <description><p>They are the top scorers in the league, they have the best goal difference and they demolished the champions</p><p>By <a href="https://www.whoscored.com/">WhoScored</a></p><p>Wingerless, without Danny Welbeck and third in the Premier League.       <title>Havertz, Isak, Dorgu … spate of injuries with national teams leaves sour taste for top clubs</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/oct/08/premier-league-injuries-kai-havertz-alexander-isak-patrick-dorgu</link>
      <description><p>Premier League clubs, and their European rivals, left with a long list of absentees after a gruelling international break</p><p>A four-match international break has presented a stress test. “The intensity of the squad, the athleticism of it, really, I think it’s designed for the elite,” said the Wales head coach, Craig Bellamy, on the completion of four matches in 11 days. Elite club coaches would disagree. The Nations League and the wider set of international games staged across the globe have been accompanied by a daily list of casualties, club officials viewing matches through their fingers as players pull up and gesture to the bench.</p><p>Hamstring and muscle problems have been rife. Sunderland, for example, will be without Brian Brobbey, a key striker, and Dan Ballard, a defensive mainstay, because of strains picked up playing for the Netherlands and Northern Ireland respectively. Bournemouth, yet to win a Premier League match, <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/oct/05/alex-scott-injury-two-months-england-bournemouth">have lost Alex Scott for up to two months</a>. His performance for England in <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/oct/03/croatia-england-nations-league-match-report">their 7-0 victory against Croatia</a> won rave reviews, a young player taking his chance and outshining Luka Modric. It came at a heavy cost. A quadriceps injury that had been diagnosed pre-match worsened. “There was zero risk taken from our side,” said Thomas Tuchel. The Bournemouth coach, Marco Rose, is unlikely to see it that way.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/oct/08/premier-league-injuries-kai-havertz-alexander-isak-patrick-dorgu">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Let there be blanks instead of Manchester City’s name on trophies: there was no honour there | Jonathan Wilson</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/oct/03/blank-instead-manchester-city-name-trophies-premier-league</link>
      <description><p>The spaces can stand both as a rebuke to an era of greed but also a tribute to the Premier League’s hunt for justice</p><p>At half-time in the 2014 League Cup final, Sunderland led Manchester City 1-0. Yaya Touré equalised with a casually brilliant 30-yard clip 10 minutes after the break, and City went on to win 3-1. City, we now know from the independent commission, were at the time involved in <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/sep/29/manchester-city-found-guilty-all-premier-league-charges-rule-breaches">a prolonged and calculated act of cheating</a>, while Touré, the leaks in Der Spiegel suggested, was being paid via a dual contract to disguise exactly how much City were spending. Although precise details were left to the appendices, the commission’s report refers to payments “not recorded in an employment contract … but instead recorded in a consultancy agreement”.</p><p>Had Sunderland won, they would not merely have ended a 41-year wait for a trophy but would have qualified for the following season’s Europa League. It’s possible, of course, that the strain the extra games placed on the squad would have led to relegation in 2015, rather than the familiar trope of sacking a manager, in this case Gus Poyet, midway through the season, and surviving thanks to a bump under his successor, Dick Advocaat.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/football/2026/oct/03/blank-instead-manchester-city-name-trophies-premier-league">Continue reading...</a></description>
